enhanced.fullText:
The Restrictions on Former Officers, Employees, and Elected Officials of the Executive and Legislative Branches, codified in 18 U.S.C. § 207, establishes comprehensive post-employment restrictions for federal government personnel to prevent conflicts of interest and maintain public trust in government operations. These regulations directly impact higher education institutions through their interactions with former federal officials who may join university administrations, serve on boards, or provide consulting services.

18 U.S.C. § 207(a) imposes a permanent bar on former federal employees from representing third parties in communications or appearances before any federal agency regarding particular matters in which they personally and substantially participated while in government service. The statute's lifetime prohibition under § 207(a)(1) applies to any matter that directly and predictably affects the financial interests of parties involved. Section 207(c) extends restrictions to senior employees, including those at GS-17 level and above, political appointees, and Senior Executive Service members, prohibiting them from representing others before their former agencies for two years post-employment.

For higher education institutions, compliance is critical when engaging former federal officials in roles involving government relations, grant applications, or regulatory advocacy. Universities must implement screening procedures under § 207(j) to identify potential conflicts before hiring former federal personnel. The Office of Government Ethics (OGE) provides interpretive guidance through 5 CFR Part 2637, clarifying that institutions may face criminal liability if they knowingly permit violations.

Violations carry severe penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 207(i), including criminal fines up to $250,000 and imprisonment up to five years for willful violations. The Department of Justice prosecutes criminal violations, while OGE handles administrative enforcement. Universities must establish compliance programs including conflict screening protocols, employee training on restriction recognition, and documentation systems for due diligence efforts.

Recent amendments through the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act strengthened disclosure requirements for senior officials. The regulation's scope encompasses all communications with federal agencies, including informal contacts and written submissions, making comprehensive compliance programs essential for higher education institutions engaging in federal advocacy or seeking government funding.
enhanced.summary: 18 U.S.C. § 207 restricts former federal officials from lobbying their former agencies, impacting universities hiring ex-government personnel for roles involving federal advocacy, grants, or regulatory matters.
enhanced.requirements:
## Core Screening Requirements
- Conduct pre-employment conflict checks for all former federal officials under 18 U.S.C. § 207(j)
- Maintain documentation of screening procedures and conflict assessments
- Implement position-specific restrictions based on former employee's government role and tenure

## Prohibited Activities Management
- Prevent lifetime bar violations under § 207(a) for particular matters with personal/substantial participation
- Enforce two-year cooling-off periods for senior officials under § 207(c)
- Monitor all federal agency communications and representations by former officials

## Training and Compliance Programs
- Develop staff training on identifying potential § 207 conflicts
- Establish clear protocols for government relations activities
- Create escalation procedures for conflict resolution

## Documentation and Monitoring
- Maintain records of all screening decisions and conflict determinations
- Track former officials' restricted activities and expiration dates
- Document compliance efforts to demonstrate good faith institutional practices
enhanced.reportingRequirements: No specific federal reporting requirements exist under 18 U.S.C. § 207 for institutions. However, universities must maintain internal documentation of screening procedures, conflict assessments, and compliance monitoring activities.
